limit: The best measured value is about 482,007,923 bps under a sender-side scheduler with TcpCubic at l1.queue.length=100; this is near the scheduler's equal-share ceiling for TCP on the 1 Gbps link, and the search was limited to the tested queue disciplines, queue lengths, and TCP types (E1, E3, E4, E5, C2, V2).
explanation: A shared FIFO or pfifofast queue lets the 2 Gbps UDP flow saturate l1 and starve TCP, giving tcp_goodput_bps=0 (E0, E2, T1, T18). A per-flow scheduler or fqcodel queue isolates TCP service, allowing loss-based TCP to fill about half the link, about 482 Mbps (E1, E2, C2, V2). Scheduler q100 with TcpCubic is preferred over fqcodel because it reaches the same tcp_goodput_bps with far fewer TCP retransmissions (E1, E2). Smaller queues cause TCP drops and lower goodput, larger queues add delay and slightly lower goodput, and delay-based BBR/Vegas underfill the scheduler share (E3, E4, E5, T8, T16, T17, T26-T30).

claims.text: Shared FIFO/pfifo service starves TCP under the 2 Gbps UDP flow.
Per-flow scheduler or fqcodel service isolates TCP and lets loss-based TCP reach about 482 Mbps.
Scheduler q100 with TcpCubic is the best tested setting; Bic, NewReno, and LinuxReno are within tolerance but not better, while BBR and Vegas underfill.
Queue length matters only through drops or added delay: q4 lowers goodput by causing TCP drops, q1000 removes drops but lowers goodput slightly.
